power.title: Communiqué on State Television
power.flavour: A general reads the numbered order on state TV. Brass bands follow.

law.title: Military Budget Beyond Oversight
law.flavour: Parliament can no longer see or touch the army's budget and businesses.

picks.title: One Hand
picks.flavour: Banners outside the state TV building say the army and people are one hand.

picks.title: Officers' Club Loyalty
picks.flavour: Dinners at the officers' clubs keep the colonels close and the barracks quiet.

picks.title: The Sofa Party
picks.flavour: Older Cairenes who watched from home fear chaos and back the man of order.

power.title: Bread Subsidy Decree
power.flavour: Flat bread stays at five piastres a loaf. The mill strikes in Mahalla pause.

law.title: Public-Sector Minimum Wage
law.flavour: A wage floor for every state clerk and mill worker, paid from shrinking reserves.

picks.title: Mahalla Strike Committees
picks.flavour: The textile workers of Mahalla talk to you before they strike.

picks.title: Bread, Freedom, Social Justice
picks.flavour: Nasser's portraits go up again in the town squares of the Delta.

picks.title: The Public-Sector Payroll
picks.flavour: Pay state wages on time, and the workers trust the state.

power.title: Release Military-Court Detainees
power.flavour: Civilians sentenced by military courts walk free past waiting cameras.

law.title: End of the Emergency Law
law.flavour: Thirty years of rule by emergency powers end with one signature.

picks.title: Free Independent Dailies
picks.flavour: Independent papers like al-Masry al-Youm print what state TV will not.

picks.title: Civilian Advisory Council
picks.flavour: Lawyers and party leaders sit beside the generals and share the blame.

picks.title: Crescent and Cross
picks.flavour: The 1919 sign of Muslim-Christian unity returns to Tahrir. Muslims and Copts march together.

power.title: Timetable Pact with the Brotherhood
power.flavour: The Brotherhood keeps its men off the square. You keep the election dates.

law.title: Parliament Writes the Constitution
law.flavour: Elected deputies choose the hundred people who draft Egypt's new constitution.

picks.title: Brotherhood Discipline
picks.flavour: The Brotherhood's small study cells turn one order into a million voters by Friday.

picks.title: Friday Sermons
picks.flavour: The mosque pulpit carries your words further than state television does.

picks.title: The Freedom and Justice Ballot
picks.flavour: While the vote stays on schedule, the Brotherhood stays off the barricades.

power.title: Sermon on Salafist Television
power.flavour: An Alexandria sheikh blesses order on al-Nas, a religious satellite channel.

law.title: Article 2 Entrenched
law.flavour: Sharia's principles stay the main source of law, and no one may amend that.

picks.title: Alexandria Lessons
picks.flavour: Salafist mosques in Alexandria teach obedience to a ruler who guards religion.

picks.title: Gulf-Printed Books
picks.flavour: Riyadh's goodwill arrives as crates of religious books and as bank deposits.

picks.title: Neighbourhood Mosque Network
picks.flavour: Young men in short robes carry the preachers' word from street to street.

centreLaws.title: The Al-Azhar Document
centreLaws.flavour: Grand Imam Ahmed el-Tayeb's charter: a democratic state, with Sharia as main source.

centreLaws.title: National Salvation Cabinet
centreLaws.flavour: Kamal Ganzouri's experts run the ministries and take the blame.

iron.title: Referral to Military Prosecutors
iron.flavour: Civilians face military judges. By year's end, twelve thousand have.

iron.title: The Maspero Line
iron.flavour: State television, at the Maspero building, reports what the Military Police decide.

iron.title: Emergency Law Renewed
iron.flavour: Emergency powers stay in force. The street learns to wait.

open.title: Tahrir's Grudging Credit
open.flavour: The protesters in the square lower one banner and give you a month.

open.title: The Election Calendar
open.flavour: Vote dates printed in the state paper keep the Brotherhood busy counting votes.

open.title: Foreign Observers Welcome
open.flavour: Foreign monitors watch the polling stations. Washington and Doha notice.

centre.title: National Dialogue Conference
centre.flavour: Every camp gets a microphone in the same hall.

centre.title: Ganzouri's Ledger
centre.flavour: A careful hand on the budget slows the loss of reserves.

centre.title: The Arbiter's Seat
centre.flavour: You stand above the camps and choose which one to hear first.

iron.title: Clear the Square
iron.flavour: Riot police trucks roll into Tahrir before dawn prayer.

iron.title: Raid the Foreign-Funded Groups
iron.flavour: Prosecutors seal the offices of foreign-funded groups and seize their files.

open.title: Free the Tahrir Detainees
open.flavour: Pardons for the young men held since the last street clashes.

open.title: Open Debate on State TV
open.flavour: Opposition leaders speak live on state television for the first time.

usa.title: The Secretary's Waiver
usa.flavour: Hillary Clinton signs, and the $1.3 billion in US military aid flows again.

ksa.title: Saudi Deposit Tranche
ksa.flavour: Another part of Riyadh's $4 billion pledge lands at the Central Bank.

qat.title: Doha's Deposit
qat.flavour: The emir's money arrives, and his channel Al Jazeera softens its coverage.

visions.name: The Guardian State
visions.line: Hand over the presidency, but keep the budget, command and veto with the army.

pillars.text: File five State Nationalist decisions.
End the term in the State Nationalist zone.
Keep the Armed Forces at 65 or more.
Hand over with grip at 60 or more.

visions.name: Bread and Sovereignty
visions.line: The Nasserist path: fair wages, cheap bread, and no foreign conditions on the republic.

pillars.text: File five Nasserist decisions.
End the term in the Nasserist zone.
Keep the Revolutionary Youth at 45 or more.

visions.name: The Civil State
visions.line: ElBaradei's road: emergency powers ended, civilians freed, a constitution for every citizen.

pillars.text: File four Liberal decisions.
End the term in the Liberal zone.
Hand over with grip at 50 or less.

visions.name: Power from the Ballot Box
visions.line: Keep every election date, let parliament write the constitution, hand power to the winners.

pillars.text: File four Islamist decisions.
End the term in the Islamist zone.
Keep the Muslim Brotherhood at 50 or more.

visions.name: Article 2 Guarded
visions.line: The Salafist Nour Party picks winners, Riyadh pays, and Sharia's place cannot be amended.

pillars.text: File four Salafist decisions.
End the term in the Salafist zone.
Keep the Salafist Call at 45 or more.

visions.name: The Arbiter's Transition
visions.line: Stand above every camp, guard the reserves, and hand over with the army's trust.

pillars.text: End the term in the centre zone.
Keep reserves at $15 billion or more.
Keep the Armed Forces at 60 or more.
Keep the Muslim Brotherhood at 45 or more.

combos.name: The Timetable Bargain
combos.why: Iron rule held steady while the Brotherhood is bought with fixed election dates.

combos.name: Ganzouri's Payroll
combos.why: Centre income in reserves converts straight into trust through the public payroll.

combos.name: Sermon and Communiqué
combos.why: Cheaper power cards make the state television communiqué cost almost nothing.

army.title: The Generals Grow Restless
army.question: Field Marshal, will you shield the army's budget or risk the officers?
army.body: The service commanders met in Nasr City without you. They want three things. The military budget sealed from parliament. No officer before a civilian court. No more soldiers sent against crowds. Lieutenant General Sami Anan has asked for a full Council session on Thursday.

answers.text: Seal the military budget from any civilian review
answers.sub: By decree, the army's businesses stay beyond parliament's reach.

reasons.army: Our factories, land and aid stay ours alone.
reasons.moi: A strong army shields the police beside it.
reasons.mb: An army above parliament makes our majority empty.
reasons.rev: A state within the state, written into law.
reasons.usa: Congress wants civilian oversight, not secret accounts.

answers.gripWhy: Ruling the budget by decree hardens your hold.

answers.text: Open the budget to an elected parliament
answers.sub: Deputies may read and vote on the defence accounts.

reasons.army: Civilian scrutiny of our budget is our red line.
reasons.rev: At last the generals answer to the people.
reasons.usa: Real civilian control, the change Washington asked for.
reasons.mb: Parliament gains power, and we will lead parliament.
reasons.fel: Open army books today, open tycoons' books tomorrow.

answers.gripWhy: Oversight of the army loosens your hold.

answers.text: Trade army autonomy for the Brotherhood's election dates
answers.sub: A quiet pact: the Brothers get votes, the barracks stay closed.

reasons.army: A partner who leaves our budget alone will do.
reasons.mb: Elections on time are all our leaders need.
reasons.salc: A Brotherhood deal leaves the Nour Party outside.
reasons.rev: The generals and the Brothers split the revolution.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh did not pay to seat the Brotherhood.

mb.title: The Brotherhood Wants Dates
mb.question: Will you fix the election date, or face the Brotherhood in Tahrir?
mb.body: Brotherhood offices in every province have hired buses. General Guide Mohamed Badie demands three things. A fixed election calendar. No more talk of charters that bind parliament. The right of the largest bloc to form a government. A Friday march to 'Hand over power' is called this week.

answers.text: Publish a fixed calendar and drop the charter
answers.sub: Votes on set dates; no binding principles over parliament.

reasons.mb: The ballot box decides everything, on our timetable.
reasons.salc: Early votes favour the Islamist parties, us included.
reasons.army: Without a charter, an elected majority can touch us.
reasons.fel: Quick elections hand the provinces to the Brotherhood.
reasons.ksa: A fast road to a Brotherhood parliament alarms Riyadh.

answers.text: Ban the march and arrest the organisers
answers.sub: Military Police at the squares; Brotherhood leaders detained.

reasons.mb: The prisons of 1954 and 1965 open again.
reasons.moi: The men we hunted for decades, back in cells.
reasons.army: The street learns who still commands it.
reasons.ksa: Exactly the firmness Riyadh expects from Cairo.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies jailed; Al Jazeera will show it all.
reasons.usa: Arresting a party running in elections worries Washington.

answers.gripWhy: Mass arrests and a march banned by order.

answers.text: Call a national dialogue of all parties
answers.sub: Liberals, Copts and youth seated beside the Brotherhood.

reasons.mb: Talk is just delay dressed up as agreement.
reasons.salc: Seated with secularists as one voice among many.
reasons.rev: At least the youth get a seat this time.
reasons.usa: Open dialogue is what Washington has been urging.
reasons.fel: Dialogue slows the Brotherhood and leaves room for us.

answers.gripWhy: Opening the table to every party eases tension.

salc.title: Hands Off Article 2
salc.question: Will you swear Article 2 stays untouched, or let secularists rewrite it?
salc.body: Article 2 makes Islamic law's principles the main source of legislation. Preachers on the al-Nas and al-Rahma channels call your constitutional plans an attack on Islam. Yasser Borhami wants a written pledge that Article 2 can never be amended. Buses from Alexandria and the Delta are booked for Friday.

answers.text: Pledge in writing that Article 2 is untouchable
answers.sub: Sharia's principles stay the source of law, sealed by you.

reasons.salc: God's law is placed beyond the secularists' reach.
reasons.mb: The Islamic basis is secured without our fighting.
reasons.rev: The Council bows to preachers, not to citizens.
reasons.usa: Washington hears the Copts' alarm in every cable.
reasons.fel: Preachers set the terms; the old business class worries.

answers.text: Insist the new constitution guarantees equal citizenship
answers.sub: Muslims and Copts equal before the law; Article 2 left open.

reasons.salc: Tampering with Article 2 is our red line.
reasons.rev: Crescent and cross, equal citizens, as in Tahrir.
reasons.usa: Equal rights for Copts reassure Congress.
reasons.mb: An open Article 2 hands secularists a weapon.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh will not watch Cairo drift from Sharia.

answers.gripWhy: A citizenship pledge opens the constitutional debate.

answers.text: Let al-Azhar's scholars settle the religion clauses
answers.sub: Al-Azhar, the state's great mosque-university, frames Article 2, not street preachers.

reasons.salc: Al-Azhar's state sheikhs never spoke for us.
reasons.mb: An Islamic basis with no Salafist veto suits us.
reasons.army: A state institution keeps religion in orderly hands.
reasons.rev: Clerics of any rank should not define citizenship.
reasons.qat: A moderate Islamic framing is what Doha backs.

moi.title: The Police Stay Home
moi.question: Will you shield police officers from trial, or let prosecutors in?
moi.body: Half of Cairo's police stations stand empty. Officers refuse to patrol while colleagues face murder charges over the January killings. Their officers' club demands three things. Stop the prosecutions. Keep State Security files sealed. Put the army behind them.

answers.text: Halt the prosecutions of officers for January
answers.sub: Cases frozen; the police return to the streets.

reasons.moi: Our men are shielded; we go back to work.
reasons.army: Police on patrol means soldiers back in barracks.
reasons.fel: Order returns, and old friends stay out of court.
reasons.rev: The killers of our martyrs walk free.
reasons.usa: Letting protesters' killers go free is Washington's red line.

answers.gripWhy: Freeing police from trial restores the old fear.

answers.text: Purge the senior ranks and restructure the ministry
answers.sub: Generals retired; State Security files opened to prosecutors.

reasons.moi: A purge of officers is our red line.
reasons.army: Purges spread; the army fears its own turn.
reasons.rev: The police state taken apart, as January demanded.
reasons.usa: Police reform is the change Washington pays for.
reasons.mb: Our old jailers lose their files and their posts.

answers.gripWhy: Breaking the security services loosens control of the street.

answers.text: Raise junior police pay, but let trials run
answers.sub: Junior police won back; commanders still face the court.

reasons.moi: The ranks are paid, though the generals still worry.
reasons.rev: Trials go on; pay is not a pardon.
reasons.army: The treasury favours police over the barracks.
reasons.fel: Old allies in the ministry still face the cage.

fel.title: The Remnants Close Ranks
fel.question: Will you block the isolation law, or let the old party's men be barred?
fel.body: Former deputies of the old ruling party, the NDP, have stopped paying workers in Sohag and Qena. Tycoons are moving dollars to Dubai. Their price is plain. No law barring old-party men from politics. No new corruption cases. Their families free to stand in the elections.

answers.text: Shelve the isolation law and new corruption cases
answers.sub: Old notables may stand; their fortunes stay untouched.

reasons.fel: Our families, money and votes stay in play.
reasons.army: The provincial notables are the army's natural allies.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh trusts the men of the old order.
reasons.rev: The old regime's men, pardoned in all but name.
reasons.mb: The old party's machine is set loose against us.

answers.text: Pass the isolation law against old-party leaders
answers.sub: Old ruling-party leaders barred from office for ten years.

reasons.fel: Barring old-party members from office is our red line.
reasons.moi: The ministry's old patrons pushed out of power.
reasons.rev: The men of the old regime cannot return.
reasons.mb: Our strongest provincial rivals leave the ballot.
reasons.usa: A clean break mostly satisfies the democracy lobby.

answers.text: Seize looted land and return it to the state
answers.sub: Tycoons' desert plots and sold-off factories taken back for the public.

reasons.fel: Losing our land and contracts means ruin.
reasons.rev: The stolen wealth goes back to the people.
reasons.army: Seizures set an example for the army's own firms.
reasons.ksa: Gulf investors in those plots lose their money.
reasons.usa: Seizing property scares every foreign investor away.

rev.title: Down With Military Rule
rev.question: Will you end military trials for civilians, or clear the square?
rev.body: Tents are back in Tahrir Square. The Revolution Youth Coalition and April 6 make three demands. No more civilians sent to military courts. The Emergency Law, which allows arrest without charge, lifted. A date for the army to leave power. Marches are called for Alexandria and Suez.

answers.text: End military trials and lift the Emergency Law
answers.sub: Civilians back before civilian judges; detainees' cases reviewed.

reasons.rev: The revolution's first demand, finally met.
reasons.usa: Ending emergency rule is the step Congress demanded.
reasons.qat: Freedom in Cairo, shown proudly on Al Jazeera.
reasons.moi: Without emergency powers our arrests mean nothing.
reasons.army: Military prosecutors were our fastest tool for order.

answers.gripWhy: You give up emergency powers and military courts.

answers.text: Clear the square with the Military Police
answers.sub: Tents torn down at dawn; organisers sent to military prosecutors.

reasons.rev: 'Down with military rule,' louder in every city.
reasons.moi: The square cleared, and the state feared again.
reasons.ksa: Order in Cairo is order in the Gulf.
reasons.army: Soldiers dragged into policing the street once more.
reasons.usa: Pictures of soldiers clearing tents reach Congress.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera's cameras will show every tent torn down.

answers.gripWhy: The square is cleared by force at dawn.

answers.text: Grant a minimum wage and receive the youth
answers.sub: A 700-pound wage floor for state workers; youth leaders received.

reasons.rev: Bread and social justice, with a seat at the table.
reasons.usa: Talks with the youth look like a real transition.
reasons.fel: Wage floors fall on employers' payrolls.
reasons.mb: The youth are courted while we are kept waiting.

usa.title: Washington Puts Terms on Aid
usa.question: Will you meet Washington's terms, or risk the $1.3 billion?
usa.body: The US embassy brings a message from the Secretary of State. Congress wants proof of a real transition before releasing $1.3 billion in military aid. It asks three things. A fixed date for the handover. American democracy groups left alone. No more protesters killed. Otherwise the aid stays frozen.

answers.text: Fix the handover date and free the aid groups
answers.sub: A public calendar; cases dropped; American staff may leave.

reasons.usa: A believable transition, and our citizens safe.
reasons.rev: A date for the generals to go, in writing.
reasons.army: Washington dictates the calendar of our exit.
reasons.moi: Foreign-funded agitators walk free despite our files.
reasons.ksa: Cairo bending to Washington's democracy agenda irritates Riyadh.

answers.gripWhy: A public handover date loosens your hold.

answers.text: Refuse orders and denounce foreign funding
answers.sub: State television attacks American meddling; the cases go ahead.

reasons.usa: Prosecuting Americans is our red line.
reasons.army: Sovereignty before aid; the army bows to no one.
reasons.moi: Our case against the foreign groups goes ahead.
reasons.ksa: Cairo standing up to Washington pleases Riyadh.
reasons.rev: Every activist is now branded a foreign agent.

answers.gripWhy: A campaign against foreign funding tightens control.

answers.text: Cancel American programmes and go it alone
answers.sub: No IMF loan, no US aid; Egypt pays its way.

reasons.usa: Cairo walks away from thirty years of partnership.
reasons.army: Without American spare parts our tanks stand still.
reasons.fel: We lose the American contracts we lived on.
reasons.rev: Independence from Washington, as Nasser would have it.
reasons.salc: No American hand in Egypt's affairs.

ksa.title: Riyadh Holds Its Deposits
ksa.question: Will you spare Mubarak and curb the Brotherhood to keep Riyadh's money?
ksa.body: Riyadh's promised deposits sit unpaid at the Central Bank. The King is angry at calls to try Mubarak. He is angry at Brotherhood leaders courting Qatar. His adviser is blunt. The money moves when Mubarak is spared and the Brotherhood held back.

answers.text: Spare Mubarak a public trial; keep him in Sharm
answers.sub: Kept in medical seclusion at Sharm el-Sheikh; no cage, no cameras.

reasons.ksa: An old friend spared shame; the deposits move.
reasons.fel: The old president spared means the old order spared.
reasons.rev: The tyrant escapes justice; Tahrir will rise again.
reasons.mb: The Council protects Mubarak and bows to Riyadh.
reasons.usa: Shielding Mubarak looks like a restoration to Congress.

answers.gripWhy: You override the demand for a trial by decree.

answers.text: Favour the Nour Party over the Brotherhood
answers.sub: Salafist preachers get airtime and licences; the Brotherhood is squeezed.

reasons.ksa: Our Salafist friends hold back Doha's Brotherhood.
reasons.salc: At last the state treats us as the Brotherhood's equal.
reasons.mb: The Council splits the Islamist camp against us.
reasons.rev: Preachers promoted while the youth are ignored.
reasons.qat: Riyadh's clients pushed ahead of Doha's allies.

answers.text: Let the courts try Mubarak like any citizen
answers.sub: Justice runs its course; Riyadh's deposits wait.

reasons.ksa: Mubarak in the dock insults the King.
reasons.fel: If Mubarak falls in court, so do his men.
reasons.rev: No one above the law, not even Mubarak.
reasons.usa: Fair trials for the old regime read well in Congress.
reasons.mb: Our old persecutor faces judgment at last.

qat.title: Al Jazeera's Cameras Turn
qat.question: Will you open the door to Doha, or shut Al Jazeera's office?
qat.body: Al Jazeera's Egypt channel, Mubasher Misr, shows every clash live, with Brotherhood guests every hour. Qatar's envoy offers investment and deposits if elections stay on time and the Brotherhood stays free. The Interior Ministry wants the Cairo office closed.

answers.text: Welcome Doha's money and keep the vote on time
answers.sub: Qatari deposits arrive; the Brotherhood's freedoms guaranteed.

reasons.qat: Our influence in Cairo grows with our money.
reasons.mb: Our Gulf friend pays, and the vote stays on schedule.
reasons.ksa: A Qatari foothold in Cairo is Riyadh's nightmare.
reasons.moi: Foreign money makes the Brotherhood untouchable.
reasons.army: Doha buys a say in Egypt's politics.

answers.text: Raid the Cairo office and seize its equipment
answers.sub: Broadcast licences pulled; the channel goes dark in Egypt.

reasons.qat: A crackdown on our channel is a crackdown on us.
reasons.mb: Our loudest platform is silenced.
reasons.moi: No more live footage of every clash.
reasons.ksa: Al Jazeera stirred the Arab street; good riddance.
reasons.usa: Raiding journalists embarrasses Washington's partner.
reasons.rev: The cameras that protected Tahrir are gone.

answers.gripWhy: A broadcaster raided and silenced by order.

answers.text: Let every channel broadcast, but refuse Doha's money
answers.sub: A free press, with no foreign deposits buying influence.

reasons.qat: Our offer refused in front of the Arab world.
reasons.mb: Our patron's money turned away at the door.
reasons.rev: Free screens, with no Gulf strings attached.
reasons.usa: Press freedom without Gulf patronage reassures Washington.
reasons.ksa: Doha shut out of Cairo's treasury pleases Riyadh.

answers.gripWhy: Every channel left free to broadcast.

elections.title: The People's Assembly Vote
elections.question: Field Marshal, will you open the polls on schedule?
elections.body: Ballot boxes and judges are ready for three rounds across 27 governorates, Egypt's provinces. The Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice lists draw the biggest rallies. The Salafist Nour Party is close behind. 498 elected seats in the lower house are at stake.

answers.text: Hold the elections on schedule, supervised by judges
answers.sub: Three rounds, judges watching, foreign observers let in.

reasons.mb: Our organisation will fill the new parliament.
reasons.salc: The Nour Party enters parliament in force.
reasons.usa: A real vote is the change Washington wanted.
reasons.fel: Without the old party machine, our clans face the Islamists.
reasons.moi: We police three rounds while the Brotherhood takes over.

answers.gripWhy: Free elections watched by judges open the field.

answers.text: Postpone the vote until order returns
answers.sub: A decree extends your rule; order first, ballots later.

reasons.mb: Cancelling the vote is our red line.
reasons.salc: Our first chance at parliament snatched away.
reasons.rev: The generals never meant to leave.
reasons.army: More time to secure the army's place first.
reasons.ksa: No Brotherhood parliament; Riyadh is relieved.

answers.gripWhy: Elections delayed by military decree.

answers.text: Draw districts to favour the old notables and clans
answers.sub: Big rural districts; old ruling-party families win single seats.

reasons.fel: Our families keep the provincial seats they always held.
reasons.army: A parliament of notables will not touch the barracks.
reasons.mb: The map is drawn to cheat us of seats.
reasons.rev: The old party returns through rigged districts.
reasons.usa: Observers will call the map rigged.

answers.gripWhy: A rigged map keeps the old order in charge.

elections.title: The Shura Council Vote
elections.question: Will you hold the upper house vote, or spare the country another ballot?
elections.body: The Shura Council, the upper house of parliament, is due to be elected in two stages. Many fear low turnout after weeks of lower house voting. The Brotherhood wants it done before the constitution-writing assembly is chosen. The generals want time.

answers.text: Hold the Shura vote and seat the upper house
answers.sub: Both houses filled; parliament may choose the constitution's writers.

reasons.mb: Both houses ours, and the constitution with them.
reasons.salc: More seats for Nour, more say on Sharia.
reasons.usa: Finishing the elected bodies keeps the timeline believable.
reasons.army: An Islamist parliament will write the constitution alone.
reasons.fel: Another round the old notables cannot win.

answers.gripWhy: Another free vote widens elected power.

answers.text: Suspend the Shura vote until the constitution is written
answers.sub: You keep a hand on who writes the constitution.

reasons.army: We shape the constitution before the Islamists can.
reasons.ksa: Slowing the Brotherhood is just what Riyadh wants.
reasons.mb: Cancelling a vote is our red line.
reasons.salc: Our seats in the upper house are taken away.
reasons.rev: Another delay, another sign the generals will stay.

answers.gripWhy: A vote suspended by your order.

elections.title: The Presidential Ballot
elections.question: Will you let the presidential vote run, or delay the handover?
elections.body: Thirteen candidates remain after the election commission's cuts. Mohamed Morsi, chairman of Freedom and Justice, has the Brotherhood machine. Ahmed Shafik has the old party's networks. Hamdeen Sabahi has the Delta towns. Farouk Sultan's commission waits for your word on the date.

answers.text: Open the polls on 23 May as promised
answers.sub: Two rounds; the winner sworn in by 30 June.

reasons.mb: The presidency is within reach of our machine.
reasons.usa: The promised handover to an elected civilian, on time.
reasons.rev: A civilian president, whatever the race's flaws.
reasons.army: An elected president may claim command of the army.
reasons.ksa: A Brotherhood president is now a real risk.

answers.gripWhy: The presidency opened to a free vote.

answers.text: Extend your mandate by a new declaration
answers.sub: Handover postponed; the generals rule six more months.

reasons.army: No civilian over us yet.
reasons.moi: The Council stays, and so does our cover.
reasons.mb: Cancelling the vote is our red line.
reasons.rev: 'Down with military rule' now rings in every square.
reasons.usa: A broken handover pledge puts the aid at risk.

answers.gripWhy: Military rule extended by decree.

answers.text: Lean on the commission to favour Shafik
answers.sub: State media, governors and counting rooms back the general.

reasons.fel: Our man in the palace, our fortunes safe.
reasons.army: A former air force commander as president suits us.
reasons.mb: A stolen presidency means we take to the street.
reasons.rev: The old regime's prime minister put in by fraud.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera will call it a counter-revolution.

answers.gripWhy: The state machine bends the count.

history.title: The First Declaration
history.question: Field Marshal, how will you run the state until elections?
history.body: Mubarak left for Sharm el-Sheikh two days ago. The 1971 constitution still stands. So does the parliament elected in the rigged 2010 vote. Tahrir Square empties slowly. The Brotherhood wants an election date. The April 6 youth movement wants a civilian council. The officers want time.

answers.text: Suspend the constitution; rule six months by decree
