situations.question: Will you enforce the ban on strikes, or recognise the new unions?
situations.body: The cabinet's decree making disruptive strikes a crime is now enforced. Strikers at Suez port face prosecution. Oil workers at Ain Sokhna are locked out. New independent unions want legal status and an end to the state-run union federation. The generals want the port cranes moving.

answers.text: Dissolve the federation; workers elect their own unions
answers.sub: State union bosses dismissed; the new unions bargain for pay.

reasons.rev: Workers finally control their own unions.
reasons.fel: Free unions mean strikes in every tycoon's plant.
reasons.army: Unions will spread into the army's own factories next.
reasons.moi: Strikers it once watched now organise legally.
reasons.mb: The Brotherhood loses a federation it hoped to inherit.

answers.gripWhy: Workers organise freely outside the state's control.

answers.text: Suspend the decree and pass a union freedom law
answers.sub: World labour standards adopted; strikes legal with notice; courts arbitrate.

reasons.usa: A union freedom law meets Washington's labour standards.
reasons.rev: The strike ban falls, though the federation survives.
reasons.fel: Legal strikes still cost the factories money.
reasons.army: Production waits on courts and notice periods.
reasons.moi: Its officers lose the decree they enforced.

answers.gripWhy: The strike ban is lifted by law.

answers.text: Keep the decree; hold new federation elections
answers.sub: One federation stays; disciplined Brotherhood slates can win it.

reasons.mb: Disciplined Brotherhood slates can win the federation.
reasons.army: Strikes stay illegal and the ports reopen.
reasons.fel: The decree protects the tycoons' production lines.
reasons.rev: The strike ban stays; only the bosses change.
reasons.salc: The Brotherhood takes a body the Salafists cannot contest.

answers.gripWhy: Strikes stay crimes while the federation changes hands.

situations.title: A Studio for Doha
situations.question: Will you license Al Jazeera's Cairo channel and take Doha's money?
situations.body: Envoys of the Emir of Qatar promise investment in Egyptian ports and housing. Al Jazeera Mubasher Misr, Qatar's live channel that broadcast every hour of Tahrir, wants a permanent Cairo licence. The Saudi embassy warns against giving Doha a foothold. The Brotherhood welcomes both.

answers.text: License the channel and accept the Emir's pledges
answers.sub: Doha gets a Cairo studio; Qatari investment is promised.

reasons.qat: A Cairo studio and an investment door for Doha.
reasons.mb: Its Qatari friends gain standing in Cairo.
reasons.rev: The channel that showed Tahrir stays on air.
reasons.ksa: A Doha foothold in Cairo is Riyadh's nightmare.
reasons.army: A foreign channel films the army every day.
reasons.moi: Al Jazeera cameras will follow every police action.

answers.text: Refuse Doha; license the Gulf religious channels instead
answers.sub: Al Jazeera refused; Salafist channels al-Nas and al-Rahma broadcast freely.

reasons.salc: The religious channels its preachers use broadcast freely.
reasons.ksa: Doha shut out, Gulf preachers welcomed: Riyadh's choice.
reasons.qat: Its flagship channel is refused in Cairo.
reasons.mb: The Brotherhood's loudest ally is silenced.
reasons.rev: One more channel refused, as under Mubarak.

answers.gripWhy: A news channel is refused its licence.

answers.text: License every channel under an independent media regulator
answers.sub: Al Jazeera licensed like all others; no state pledges attached.

reasons.rev: An independent regulator ends state control of broadcasting.
reasons.usa: A free media law is what Washington asked for.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera licensed, though with no favours for Doha.
reasons.ksa: Al Jazeera licensed is a Doha foothold all the same.
reasons.army: The army loses its grip on what Egyptians watch.
reasons.moi: State censors lose control of the airwaves.

answers.gripWhy: Broadcast licences pass from the state to a regulator.

situations.title: The Fund's Conditions
situations.question: Will you sign the IMF's $3 billion loan and accept its conditions?
situations.body: The IMF, the international lender, offers a $3 billion loan, with Washington's blessing. Reserves have lost $5 billion since February. Its conditions touch fuel subsidies and state firms. The generals bristle. Mubarak-era businessmen want it signed this month.

answers.text: Sign the loan and accept its reforms
answers.sub: IMF money flows; subsidies and state firms face review.

reasons.usa: The loan Washington blessed is signed, with reforms.
reasons.fel: Markets steady and investors return.
reasons.army: IMF auditors will ask about state and army firms.
reasons.rev: Putting bread and fuel subsidies on the table betrays the poor.
reasons.salc: Debt with interest is usury, forbidden in Islam.

answers.text: Refuse it; no foreign hand on bread and fuel
answers.sub: Subsidies and state firms untouched; reserves keep falling.

reasons.army: No foreign auditors near the army's businesses.
reasons.rev: Subsidies stay; the poor are spared.
reasons.mb: No loan for an elected government to inherit.
reasons.usa: Refusing the Fund rebuffs Washington's offer.
reasons.fel: Falling reserves will hit their imports and the pound.

answers.text: Refuse interest-bearing loans; ask Gulf brothers for Islamic finance
answers.sub: No debt with interest; Saudi deposits sought instead.

reasons.salc: No usury, and Gulf brothers stand by Egypt.
reasons.ksa: Cairo turns to Riyadh's money, not Washington's.
reasons.mb: The Brotherhood shares the objection to interest.
reasons.usa: Cairo rebuffs the Fund for Gulf charity.
reasons.fel: Gulf money comes slowly; markets wanted the IMF's approval.

situations.title: Seats or Lists
situations.question: Individual seats or party lists: which law will you sign?
situations.body: Mamdouh Shahin's draft election law is on your desk. Seats won by individual candidates favour the provincial families of the old ruling party, with their clans and cash. Party lists favour the disciplined Brotherhood. The youth coalition is still forming parties and begs for more time.

answers.text: Keep individual seats, as under the old republic
answers.sub: Local notables and clans carry the provinces; parties come second.

reasons.fel: Clans and cash win individual seats; the old elite returns.
reasons.army: Familiar notables make a parliament the army can manage.
reasons.moi: Provincial police know these families well.
reasons.mb: Individual seats blunt the Brotherhood's party machine.
reasons.rev: The old ruling party's families walk back into parliament.
reasons.salc: New Salafist parties cannot win clan seats.

answers.gripWhy: The old electoral machine survives intact.

answers.text: Adopt full party lists for every seat
answers.sub: Organised parties win; the Brotherhood's machine is unrivalled.

reasons.mb: Party lists turn the Brotherhood's discipline into seats.
reasons.salc: A new Salafist party can win seats on lists.
reasons.qat: Doha's Brotherhood friends head for parliament.
reasons.fel: Without individual seats, the clans lose their parliament.
reasons.army: An Islamist parliament threatens the Council's control.

answers.text: Delay the vote and adopt a mixed system
answers.sub: Half lists, half seats; elections pushed back months.

reasons.rev: Time to build parties before the Brotherhood sweeps.
reasons.usa: A slower, mixed vote looks more credible abroad.
reasons.army: More months for the Council to shape the transition.
reasons.mb: Delay is the old trick; the Brotherhood wants the vote now.
reasons.salc: Every month of delay favours the secular parties.

situations.title: Fire at the Shrines
situations.question: The shrines burn. Will you guard them, or leave the preachers alone?
situations.body: Zealots have smashed saints' tombs revered by Sufi mystics in Qalyubia and burnt a shrine in Alexandria. Grand Imam Ahmed el-Tayeb of al-Azhar, Egypt's highest Islamic authority, asks the state to guard every shrine. The Salafist Call disowns the attacks but defends preaching against grave worship. Police ask for orders.

answers.text: Let the Salafist sheikhs police their own youth
answers.sub: No arrests; the Call disciplines zealots and keeps its pulpits.

reasons.salc: The Call keeps its pulpits and polices its own.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's friends among the preachers are trusted.
reasons.moi: The street belongs to sheikhs, not officers.
reasons.army: Order handed to preachers looks like a state in retreat.
reasons.rev: Shrines burn and nobody is arrested.

answers.gripWhy: Police stand back; preachers keep order themselves.

answers.text: Call a council of Azhar, Sufi and Salafist scholars
answers.sub: The Brotherhood's moderate preachers broker a code for mosques.

reasons.mb: The Brotherhood plays the centrist broker of Islam.
reasons.qat: Doha's favoured scholars gain a national stage.
reasons.salc: A code of conduct fences in Salafist preaching.
reasons.moi: Clerics, not police, settle a security matter.
reasons.rev: Clerics negotiate while shrines burn.

answers.text: Post police on the shrines and arrest the attackers
answers.sub: Riot police guard shrines; attackers go into State Security files.

reasons.moi: Its officers return to guard posts with full authority.
reasons.army: Order restored without soldiers on the street.
reasons.fel: Order in the provinces calms the old notables.
reasons.salc: State Security files on preachers are reopened.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh dislikes Salafist preachers in Egyptian jails.

answers.gripWhy: State Security, the political police, reopens files on preachers.

situations.title: Al-Azhar's Document
situations.question: Will you make al-Azhar's Document the shared basis of the constitution?
situations.body: Al-Azhar's Document on the Future of Egypt backs a modern, democratic, constitutional state. It makes Sharia principles, the broad aims of Islamic law, the main source of laws. The Brotherhood endorses it. Salafist preachers distrust its 'modern state'. The revolutionaries are split: a civil charter, or a cleric's veto?

answers.text: Adopt the Document as the constitution's agreed basis
answers.sub: Sharia principles and a democratic state, as al-Azhar wrote.

reasons.mb: Sharia principles and the ballot: the Brotherhood's own formula.
reasons.usa: A democratic, constitutional state reassures Washington.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies win a shared charter.
reasons.salc: Its 'modern state' smuggles secularism past Article 2.
reasons.rev: A cleric's charter decides what the people should write.

answers.text: Amend it: Sharia's rulings, not just its principles
answers.sub: Strict Sharia wording; senior scholars review every law.

reasons.salc: Sharia's rulings, not vague principles, bind the state.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh welcomes a stricter Sharia clause.
reasons.mb: The Salafists outbid the Brotherhood on religion.
reasons.rev: A clerical veto over a civil state is unacceptable.
reasons.usa: Washington hears theocracy in the constitution's basis.
reasons.fel: Strict Sharia frightens tourism and business.

answers.text: Fold it into a National Charter, like Nasser's 1962
answers.sub: The state writes it: social justice, Arab identity, Azhar consulted.

reasons.army: The state, not clerics or parties, sets the charter.
reasons.rev: Social justice written into the founding charter.
reasons.mb: The state, not elected deputies, would author the constitution.
reasons.salc: Arab nationalism sidelines Sharia once again.
reasons.fel: Social justice clauses threaten privatised fortunes.

answers.gripWhy: The state, not parliament, sets the founding charter.

situations.title: Staging Mubarak's Trial
situations.question: Field Marshal, where will you put your old commander on trial?
situations.body: Hosni Mubarak is held in a Sharm el-Sheikh hospital. The charges name him with Habib el-Adly, his interior minister, and six police commanders. Riyadh's envoys ask for dignity. The families of those killed camp in Tahrir. They want him in the defendants' cage at the Police Academy, on live television.

answers.text: Try him quietly in Sharm el-Sheikh, no cameras.
answers.sub: Closed hearings by a hospital bed; the state keeps its dignity.

reasons.army: A field marshal is not paraded; the uniform keeps its honour.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's request honoured: the old ally spared humiliation.
reasons.fel: Our patron is spared the cage; our own trials may soften.
reasons.rev: A secret trial in a resort is no trial at all.
reasons.mb: Closed doors let the old regime bargain for its own.
reasons.usa: Hidden proceedings look like impunity to Congress.

answers.gripWhy: Courts closed to press and public.

answers.text: Cage him at the Police Academy, cameras live.
answers.sub: Open trial in Cairo; state television broadcasts every session.

reasons.rev: The pharaoh in a cage: proof of the revolution on screen.
reasons.usa: Open justice on camera answers critics in Congress.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera will carry every session to the Arab world.
reasons.ksa: Mubarak caged on television insults the King's friend.
reasons.moi: Six of our commanders shown to the nation as killers.
reasons.army: The cage reminds officers who might stand in it next.

answers.gripWhy: Justice opened to the public eye.

answers.text: Cage him in Cairo and seize the family fortune.
answers.sub: The Mubarak family's assets frozen and claimed for the treasury.

reasons.rev: Trial and restitution: the stolen billions come home.
reasons.mb: The plundered wealth of Egypt returns to its people.
reasons.fel: If his fortune falls, every tycoon's fortune is next.
reasons.ksa: Stripping a former president shames every Gulf friend.
reasons.army: Asset seizures invite questions about the military economy.

situations.title: The Friday of Kandahar
situations.question: Field Marshal, will you thank the sheikhs or curb their slogans?
situations.body: On 29 July Tahrir filled with Salafist banners, Saudi flags and the chant 'Islamic, Islamic'. Liberal parties walked out. They call it the 'Friday of Kandahar', after the Taliban's city. The Salafist Call says its stewards kept perfect order. The Saudi embassy counts its friends.

answers.text: Praise the Salafist Call's discipline on state television.
answers.sub: State TV thanks the sheikhs; their banners stay in the square.

reasons.salc: The state finally names us a pillar of order.
reasons.ksa: Our friends praised in Cairo, and our flag tolerated.
reasons.rev: The Council courts the bearded preachers to drown out Tahrir.
reasons.mb: Praising the Salafists splits the Islamist vote away from us.
reasons.usa: Washington sees Saudi flags blessed by the generals.
reasons.fel: Pulpit power in the provinces threatens our clans' votes.

answers.text: Ban religious slogans and foreign flags at rallies.
answers.sub: A civil-state rule for squares and campaigns, enforced by police.

reasons.rev: A civil state needs civil squares; this is a start.
reasons.usa: Rules for a pluralist campaign reassure the State Department.
reasons.moi: Clear rules give our officers grounds to clear squares.
reasons.salc: Banning God's word in God's country attacks Islam itself.
reasons.mb: Slogan bans will be turned against 'Islam is the solution'.
reasons.ksa: Our flag treated as contraband by the Council we fund.

answers.gripWhy: Police enforce limits on rally speech.

situations.title: Blood on the Eilat Border
situations.question: Five border policemen are dead. How will you answer Israel?
situations.body: On 18 August Israeli forces chasing raiders after attacks near Eilat shot five Egyptian border policemen. Crowds surround the Israeli embassy in Giza; a young man tore down its flag. Nasserists and Brotherhood leaders demand changes to the peace treaty. Washington urges calm.

answers.text: Expel the ambassador and halt gas to Israel.
answers.sub: Recall Cairo's envoy, close the pipeline, defy Washington.

reasons.rev: Egyptian blood finally answered with Egyptian dignity.
reasons.mb: The Zionist entity learns the Mubarak era is over.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera's heroes: Cairo stands up to Israel.
reasons.usa: Expelling Israel's envoy shakes the peace America underwrites.
reasons.army: Escalation risks the treaty, the aid and a Sinai war.
reasons.fel: Halted gas contracts drag our partners before prosecutors.

answers.text: Demand an apology and send troops into Sinai.
answers.sub: Israel must accept extra battalions beyond the treaty's limits.

reasons.army: More battalions in Sinai, with Israel's consent, restore command.
reasons.usa: Firm but within the treaty: exactly what Washington asked.
reasons.moi: Sinai order returns; our border men are avenged.
reasons.rev: An apology request is the old regime's whisper.
reasons.mb: Troops chase Bedouin while Israel keeps its embassy.

answers.gripWhy: Sinai placed under army operations.

answers.text: Promise the elected parliament will review the treaty.
answers.sub: Treaty kept for now; its annexes go to the people's deputies.

reasons.mb: The ballot will decide Egypt's foreign policy, as we demand.
reasons.qat: An elected Egypt reviewing Camp David suits Doha well.
reasons.salc: A review of the peace treaty answers the mosques' anger.
reasons.usa: Handing Camp David to an Islamist parliament alarms Washington.
reasons.army: Handing treaty policy to parties invades the army's domain.
reasons.ksa: A Brotherhood parliament steering foreign policy worries Riyadh.

situations.title: Summoned for a Post
situations.question: Will you let your military prosecutors try a blogger?
situations.body: The No to Military Trials campaign counts nearly 12,000 civilians tried by military courts since February. Now an activist of the April 6 youth movement is summoned to military prosecutors in Nasr City. The charge: posts accusing the Council of betraying the revolution. Washington and rights groups demand civilian courts.

answers.text: Drop the summons; send civilians to civilian courts.
answers.sub: No more military courts for civilians; pending cases go to judges.

reasons.rev: Our comrades leave the military docks; Tahrir wins.
reasons.usa: Civilian justice is the reform Congress was promised.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera praises a Council that heeds its critics.
reasons.mb: Our members remember military courts; ending them is justice.
reasons.army: The military judiciary stripped of its reach over agitators.
reasons.moi: The thugs and looters we arrest will walk free.

answers.gripWhy: Thousands of cases leave the generals' courts.

answers.text: Let the military prosecutor proceed. Insults have limits.
answers.sub: The summons stands; online criticism of the army stays a crime.

reasons.army: Nobody insults the institution that saved the revolution.
reasons.moi: Order on the internet as on the street.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh likes generals who silence troublemakers.
reasons.rev: Military trials for a post: the old regime in uniform.
reasons.usa: Prosecuting bloggers in military courts embarrasses the aid Washington gives.

answers.gripWhy: Criticism of the army becomes a military offence.

situations.title: The Nation on Strike
situations.question: Teachers, doctors and drivers are out. Will you break them, pay, or bargain?
situations.body: Schools reopened in September to empty classrooms. Teachers, public-hospital doctors and Cairo bus drivers walk out for higher pay and permanent contracts. The Brotherhood-led Doctors' Union backs them. Reserves stand at $24 billion. The cabinet's ban on strikes sits unenforced.

answers.text: Enforce the strike ban; arrest the ringleaders.
answers.sub: Military police clear bus depots; organisers face prison.

reasons.army: Production and order matter more than wage slogans.
reasons.fel: Strikes ruin business; finally the state protects it.
reasons.moi: Our men back on the beat against agitators.
reasons.rev: Jailing strikers is Mubarak's method in a new uniform.
reasons.mb: Our unions' doctors arrested: the Council declares war.
reasons.usa: Arrested teachers make poor news for a transition.

answers.gripWhy: Strikers jailed under the ban on strikes.

answers.text: Pay the raises and recognise the independent unions.
answers.sub: Raises paid from reserves; the state federation loses its monopoly.

reasons.rev: Bread and social justice delivered, not just promised.
reasons.mb: The unions win; our doctors take the credit.
reasons.fel: Wage bills and new unions threaten every factory we own.
reasons.usa: IMF hopes fade as the wage bill swells.
reasons.army: Independent unions will reach the army's factories next.

answers.gripWhy: Independent unions legally recognised.

answers.text: Settle through the Brotherhood's unions; they end the strikes.
answers.sub: Union leaders negotiate raises and call members back to work.

reasons.mb: The Council needs our unions; the state sees our weight.
reasons.qat: Doha's friends become the Council's partners.
reasons.rev: The Brotherhood sells the strikers for a seat at the table.
reasons.salc: The Brotherhood grows fat on state favours again.
reasons.moi: The Brotherhood we hunted now brokers labour peace.

situations.title: Seats for the Parties
situations.question: Field Marshal, will you change your election law by decree, or hold firm?
situations.body: Your election law keeps a third of the seats for independents. Party members cannot run for them. The Brotherhood's party and its allies threaten to boycott the vote. They want party men allowed in those seats and old ruling-party leaders barred. Registration opens within weeks.

answers.text: Decree it: parties run everywhere, old party barred.
answers.sub: Party members may run for any seat; old ruling-party leaders barred.

reasons.mb: Our candidates can run for every seat in every province.
reasons.rev: Barring the old ruling party is what the revolution demanded.
reasons.fel: Our clans lose their seats to party machines, our men barred.
reasons.army: Giving in to boycott threats teaches parties to bully the Council.
reasons.moi: Our old allies in the provinces lose their seats.

answers.text: Hold firm: keep independents' seats and the workers-farmers half.
answers.sub: Nasser's rule giving workers and farmers half the seats stays.

reasons.fel: Our village notables keep their seats by running as 'farmers'.
reasons.army: The Council's law stands; parties learn who decides.
reasons.mb: A boycott becomes our answer to an unfair map.
reasons.rev: The old party's men walk back in as independents.
reasons.qat: Doha sees the Brotherhood shut out by an old law.

answers.text: Open every seat to all parties, religious ones included.
answers.sub: Salafist Nour Party runs everywhere; old party men not barred.

reasons.salc: Our Nour Party can field preachers in every district.
reasons.mb: Party seats open, though the old men stay in.
reasons.ksa: Salafist candidates everywhere suit Riyadh's friends.
reasons.rev: No bar on the old party: the revolution betrayed.
reasons.usa: Washington worries about a ballot dominated by religious parties.

situations.title: Al Jazeera's Cairo Office
situations.question: Doha protests the raid. Will you shut its channel for good?
situations.body: On 11 September police raided the Cairo office of Al Jazeera Mubasher Misr, Qatar's Egypt channel. They seized its equipment and arrested an engineer for broadcasting without a licence. Doha protests. The Brotherhood and the youth cry censorship. The Information Ministry wants the channel closed for good.

answers.text: Shut the channel for good: Egypt's airwaves are ours.
answers.sub: No licence, equipment kept, Nilesat satellite told to drop it.

reasons.ksa: Doha's megaphone silenced in Cairo, as Riyadh hoped.
reasons.army: A foreign channel stirring people against the army is gone.
reasons.moi: No more live pictures of our men in the streets.
reasons.qat: Our channel banned: the Council takes Riyadh's side.
reasons.mb: The only screen that showed our rallies goes dark.
reasons.rev: Today Al Jazeera, tomorrow every independent camera.

answers.gripWhy: A foreign broadcaster banned.

answers.text: Return the equipment and license it under open rules.
answers.sub: One clear licensing law for all channels, foreign and private.

reasons.qat: Al Jazeera stays in Cairo, and Doha keeps its friends.
reasons.usa: Press freedom respected: the transition looks real.
reasons.rev: Cameras keep the Council honest.
reasons.ksa: Doha's channel licensed to stir Cairo against order.
reasons.army: A foreign channel licensed to film the army's mistakes.

answers.gripWhy: Licences for broadcasters opened up.

answers.text: Keep Al Jazeera off; bring back the Salafist channels.
answers.sub: Al-Nas and al-Rahma, shut in 2010, return; Doha's stays off.

reasons.salc: Our preachers return to every satellite dish.
reasons.ksa: Gulf-funded sheikhs on air, Doha's channel off: ideal.
reasons.qat: Doha silenced while Salafist sheikhs get the airwaves.
reasons.rev: Sermons licensed, journalism banned: what revolution?
reasons.mb: Salafist channels will take voters away from us.

answers.gripWhy: Picking who gets licensed keeps a foreign channel off air.

situations.title: Voting amid Tear Gas
situations.question: The polls open in nine days. Will you keep the date?
situations.body: Since 19 November, Mohamed Mahmoud Street has burned. Al Jazeera shows the tear gas live, and dozens are dead. The youth and liberal parties want the 28 November vote postponed. The Brotherhood stays off the street and insists on the date. The police doubt they can guard the polls.

answers.text: Open the polls on 28 November, as promised.
answers.sub: The ballot box answers the street; the timetable does not move.

reasons.mb: Our machine is ready; the vote ends military rule properly.
reasons.qat: Elections the Brotherhood will win, on time.
reasons.salc: The Nour Party's volunteers are in every village.
reasons.rev: Voting while friends die on Mohamed Mahmoud betrays them.
reasons.moi: Our men stretched between burning streets and polling stations.

answers.gripWhy: A national vote opens up politics.

answers.text: Postpone the vote; pull the police out of Tahrir.
answers.sub: Police withdrawn, an inquiry opened, the vote delayed two months.

reasons.rev: Blood stops the vote until the killers answer.
reasons.usa: Congress cares more about stopping the shooting than a date.
reasons.mb: Postponing a vote is our red line; Tahrir will fill.
reasons.salc: Delay robs the Islamist movement of its due.
reasons.moi: Pulling back under fire humiliates every officer.

answers.gripWhy: Police pulled back and the street left to protesters.

answers.text: Vote on time; mosque volunteers guard the polling stations.
answers.sub: Salafist neighbourhood groups guard polling stations beside the army.

reasons.salc: Our young men guard the vote: the nation sees our order.
reasons.ksa: Pious volunteers keeping order suit Riyadh.
reasons.mb: The vote goes ahead, though the Salafists take the credit.
reasons.moi: Bearded vigilantes doing our job at the ballot box.
reasons.rev: Islamist militias at the polls: the vote is theirs.
reasons.usa: Religious groups at polling stations alarm observers.

situations.title: A Salvation Government
situations.question: Sharaf has resigned. Whom will you name to lead the cabinet?
situations.body: Prime Minister Essam Sharaf's government resigned on 21 November during the Mohamed Mahmoud clashes. Tahrir chants for Mohamed ElBaradei, the former UN nuclear chief, to lead a 'national salvation government' with full powers. Your own men favour Kamal Ganzouri, Mubarak's prime minister in the 1990s. The Brotherhood keeps its distance.

answers.text: Appoint ElBaradei with full powers over the cabinet.
answers.sub: A civilian rescue government; the Council keeps only defence.

reasons.rev: Our man, with real powers: the revolution enters the state.
reasons.usa: A Nobel prize winner as premier reassures Washington.
reasons.army: Full powers for ElBaradei empty out the Council itself.
reasons.mb: A liberal premier now steals our coming election victory.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh distrusts a premier from Tahrir with full powers.

answers.gripWhy: Executive power passes to a civilian with full powers.

answers.text: Name Ganzouri, the planner of subsidies and public works.
answers.sub: A veteran state-economy premier promising bread prices and wages first.

reasons.army: A loyal technocrat who leaves the Council in charge.
reasons.fel: A familiar face from the old cabinets protects our deals.
reasons.mb: Ganzouri is temporary; parliament will soon choose.
reasons.rev: Mubarak's prime minister as the answer to our martyrs?
reasons.usa: An old-regime premier shows the Council won't let go.

situations.title: Setting the Handover Date
situations.question: Field Marshal, will you name the day you hand over power?
situations.body: You promised six months in February; they ran out in August. Tahrir chants 'Down with military rule'. Washington wants a date for the presidential election. The Brotherhood wants parliament seated first. The generals want time to secure the army's place before a civilian takes the palace.

answers.text: Keep your rule open-ended until stability returns.
answers.sub: No date; the Council hands over when the state is safe.

reasons.army: Time to write the army's place into the constitution.
reasons.ksa: An army in charge, with no deadline, keeps Egypt steady.
reasons.moi: Firm rule gives our men cover to return to the streets.
reasons.rev: Military rule with no end: Mubarak without Mubarak.
reasons.mb: No date means the Council plans to stay.
reasons.usa: No end date puts the aid at risk in Congress.

answers.gripWhy: Military rule extended without limit.

answers.text: Parliament first, then a president by June.
answers.sub: Deputies seated in January; presidential vote by the end of June.

reasons.mb: Our order exactly: the ballot box seats us first.
reasons.usa: A firm date for civilian rule, as Washington demanded.
reasons.qat: An elected Islamist parliament, then the palace: Doha's hope.
reasons.rev: The Brotherhood's timetable, and the generals keep months more.
reasons.army: A fixed exit leaves little time to protect our budget.
reasons.ksa: Brotherhood deputies first, then a president: Riyadh's nightmare.

answers.gripWhy: A date for civilian rule.

situations.title: Flowers for Faces
situations.question: Field Marshal, will you let the pulpits campaign, or ban religious slogans?
situations.body: Posters in Alexandria of the Nour Party, the Salafists' new party, show a rose where its women candidates' faces should be. Friday sermons in Kafr el-Sheikh name the party's list. Liberal parties ask for a ban on religious slogans. Brotherhood organisers say the Salafists are taking their mosques.

answers.text: Let the preachers speak; faith is no crime.
answers.sub: The pulpit stays open; no ruling on slogans.

reasons.salc: Our sheikhs reach voters the Brotherhood never could.
reasons.mb: Salafist sermons take our own voters from our mosques.
reasons.rev: Mosques turned into campaign offices; the revolution drowns.
reasons.usa: Washington wants a vote that looks like a civil contest.
reasons.ksa: Preachers Riyadh admires get a free hearing.

answers.text: Enforce the ban on religious slogans in campaigns.
answers.sub: The election commission fines posters and sermons; mosques stay out.

reasons.rev: At last the vote is about programmes, not paradise.
reasons.usa: A civil campaign is the transition promised to Congress.
reasons.salc: Silencing the pulpit is war on the call to God.
reasons.mb: 'Islam is the solution' is our slogan; the ban hits us.
reasons.fel: Old-party candidates gain when the sheikhs fall quiet.

answers.gripWhy: Inspectors police sermons and tear down posters.

answers.text: Allow general Islamic slogans; ban attacks on other faiths.
answers.sub: The Brotherhood's slogan stays; Nour's harshest sermons are reined in.

reasons.mb: Our slogan survives and Salafist excesses are curbed.
reasons.salc: A rule cut to the Brotherhood's measure, against us.
reasons.rev: Religion still rules the campaign, only more politely.
reasons.qat: Doha's friends in the Brotherhood keep their edge.
reasons.ksa: The Brotherhood favoured over Riyadh's Salafist friends.

situations.title: The Woman in the Street
situations.question: The footage is everywhere, Field Marshal. Will you apologise or blame infiltrators?
situations.body: Military police cleared the sit-in outside the cabinet office on Qasr al-Aini Street. Al Jazeera shows soldiers beating protesters and dragging a veiled woman across the road. Hillary Clinton, US Secretary of State, condemns it. Thousands of women march to Tahrir. State television blames paid infiltrators.

answers.text: Apologise to Egypt's women; send soldiers to investigators.
answers.sub: A Council apology on air; soldiers handed to investigators.

reasons.rev: An apology is the first crack in the generals' immunity.
reasons.usa: The apology Clinton demanded, and a case Congress can see.
reasons.army: Offering soldiers up to the cameras humiliates the uniform.
reasons.moi: Today soldiers, tomorrow our officers in the dock.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera wins the story and the apology.

answers.gripWhy: The Council admits fault and opens its ranks to inquiry.

answers.text: Blame paid infiltrators and foreign hands on state television.
answers.sub: State television airs 'thug' confessions; no soldier is charged.

reasons.army: No soldier sacrificed; the uniform stands untouched.
reasons.moi: The infiltrator story covers our ranks as well.
reasons.rev: They dragged our sister and call us the thugs.
reasons.usa: Aid to an army that lies on camera cannot be defended.
reasons.fel: We applaud a firm Council that puts order first.

answers.gripWhy: The army's story forced onto the airwaves; critics branded foreign.

answers.text: Compensate the wounded and promise jobs for the young.
answers.sub: Cash for victims' families; Ganzouri promises public-sector hiring.

reasons.rev: Money for blood; they buy silence, not justice.
reasons.army: No soldier charged, and the treasury pays the bill.
reasons.mb: The street calms and the Brotherhood spends nothing.
reasons.fel: Handouts drain the state while investors wait.
reasons.usa: Cash is not accountability.

situations.title: The Advisory Council
situations.question: The Brotherhood walked out. Will you let your advisers shape the assembly?
situations.body: You created a 30-member Advisory Council of public figures. It proposes how to choose the constituent assembly, the body that will write the constitution. The Brotherhood's party pulled out within days: only elected deputies may choose, it says. Liberal and old-party advisers want quotas to limit the Islamist majority.

answers.text: Leave the choice to the elected deputies alone.
answers.sub: The advisers lose the file; parliament picks all 100 members.

reasons.mb: The ballot box decides, as the March declaration promised.
reasons.salc: Our 123 seats get their share of the pen.
reasons.rev: Two Islamist parties will write a constitution for all.
reasons.fel: We lose every brake on the Islamists.
reasons.army: A constitution written without us may reach our budget.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies get to write the constitution.

answers.text: Let advisers reserve seats for women, Copts and professions.
answers.sub: Seats kept for unions, churches and jurists from outside parliament.

reasons.rev: A constitution for all Egyptians, not one bloc.
reasons.usa: Inclusive drafting is what Washington asked for.
reasons.mb: Unelected men binding the people's deputies is our red line.
reasons.salc: Seats for churches and secularists weaken Article 2's defenders.
reasons.fel: Our men sit among the advisers and the professions.

answers.text: Let the Advisory Council report only to you.
answers.sub: Advisers counsel you privately; the rules come by decree.

reasons.army: The generals keep the last word on the constitution.
reasons.mb: Council decrees placed above the elected house.
reasons.rev: Another military committee in civilian clothes.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh prefers generals keeping the Brotherhood in check.
reasons.moi: A strong Council means a protected ministry.

answers.gripWhy: Constitution rules set by decree, not by the elected house.

situations.title: The IMF Returns
situations.question: Ganzouri wants the IMF loan back. Will you put your name behind it?
situations.body: Kamal Ganzouri reopens talks with the IMF, the world's emergency lender. Its $3 billion loan was cancelled in June. Reserves have slid to about $18 billion. The IMF wants wide political backing. The Brotherhood won't endorse a debt it may inherit. Unions fear cuts to bread and fuel subsidies.

answers.text: Refuse the IMF; defend subsidies and the public sector.
answers.sub: No IMF terms; subsidies untouched while reserves keep falling.

reasons.rev: No foreign bankers setting the price of bread.
reasons.mb: We inherit no unpopular debt.
reasons.fel: Investors flee a state that refuses every rescue.
reasons.usa: Washington's offer turned down a second time.
reasons.army: No IMF inspectors near the army's businesses.

answers.text: Sign with the IMF; cut subsidies step by step.
answers.sub: $3 billion on IMF terms: fuel subsidies trimmed, deficit capped.

reasons.usa: A credible plan, with Washington's vote on the IMF board.
reasons.fel: The pound steadies and the stock exchange breathes.
reasons.rev: The poor pay for the crisis while bankers smile.
reasons.mb: We will not inherit the Council's austerity.
reasons.army: IMF auditors will ask about state companies.

answers.text: Make the loan wait for the elected parliament's consent.
answers.sub: Talks continue; signing only after the People's Assembly votes.

reasons.mb: Nothing binds us until our deputies decide.
reasons.salc: The people's house, not Ganzouri, judges the debt.
reasons.fel: Months of waiting while the pound bleeds.
reasons.usa: Giving it to an Islamist parliament puts the plan in doubt.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh dislikes handing the Brotherhood the purse.

situations.title: The Islamic Bonds Bill
situations.question: Nour wants Islamic bonds sold to the Gulf. Will you let the bill pass?
situations.body: Nour Party deputies table a bill for sukuk, Islamic bonds that pay no interest, backed by state assets. They promise Saudi and Qatari buyers by the billion. The Central Bank warns against pledging public land to foreigners. The tycoons call it amateur finance. The Brotherhood fears losing ground on faith.

answers.text: Back the sukuk bill and invite Gulf buyers.
answers.sub: Islamic bonds on state assets; religious scholars approve each issue.

reasons.salc: Islamic finance in law: Sharia enters the treasury.
reasons.ksa: Saudi banks gain a door into Egyptian assets.
reasons.mb: Nour takes credit for Islamic economics before us.
reasons.fel: Clerics running the debt scares serious money.
reasons.rev: State land pawned to Gulf princes.

answers.text: Keep state assets national; sell bonds only at home.
answers.sub: Egyptian state bonds; no foreign claim on land or canal.

reasons.rev: Egypt's land is not collateral for Gulf princes.
reasons.army: No foreigner gets a claim near military land.
reasons.salc: The people's Islamic choice traded for socialist bonds.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's capital shut out of Egypt again.
reasons.fel: State bonds swallow the credit our businesses need.

answers.text: Send it to the Central Bank for market rules.
answers.sub: Central Bank experts redraft it: no scholars' board, any buyer.

reasons.fel: Professional bankers, not preachers, manage the debt.
reasons.usa: Open markets, the reform Washington's economists want.
reasons.salc: Without the scholars' board the bill is empty.
reasons.mb: Islamic finance delayed again by the old bankers.
reasons.qat: Doha wanted an Islamic bond for its money.

situations.title: Sixteen Billion
situations.question: Reserves are near $16 billion. Will you pay the Brotherhood's price for the loan?
situations.body: Reserves stand near $16 billion, enough for about three months of imports. The Central Bank governor cannot hold up the pound much longer. The pound may crash and imports be rationed. The IMF team is back and wants parliament's backing. The Brotherhood will vote yes only if Ganzouri's cabinet goes.

answers.text: Ration imports and defend bread, not the IMF's terms.
answers.sub: Import licences, no IMF deal; wheat and fuel come first.

reasons.rev: Bread before bankers, at last.
reasons.army: No IMF and no Brotherhood cabinet; the state holds.
reasons.fel: Import licences strangle our trade and dealerships.
reasons.usa: Washington's lifeline refused a third time.
reasons.mb: Our price ignored, and the crisis left to us.

answers.gripWhy: Licences and rationing put trade under state command.

answers.text: Pay the price: a Brotherhood cabinet for its vote.
answers.sub: Ganzouri goes; Brotherhood ministers back the loan in parliament.

reasons.mb: We govern, and the loan becomes ours to shape.
reasons.qat: Doha's partners take the ministries.
reasons.army: Brotherhood ministers will reach for our accounts.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh sees the Brotherhood handed the state.
reasons.fel: Our men lose the cabinet to the Islamists.

answers.text: Let the pound fall and sign the experts' deal.
answers.sub: Pound lowered on IMF terms; Ganzouri stays, parliament bypassed.

reasons.usa: A real programme, backed by the IMF board.
reasons.fel: A free pound lets investors return.
reasons.mb: Signing over our heads breaks the people's mandate.
reasons.rev: Prices jump overnight for every family.
reasons.salc: A loan with interest, signed without the people's deputies.

situations.title: The Red Line
situations.question: The defence committee wants the army's books. Will you open them?
situations.body: Brotherhood deputies on parliament's defence committee ask to review the military budget line by line. They also want the army's factories, hotels and land put on the record. Sami Anan, the army chief of staff, calls it the red line. American diplomats privately favour oversight.

answers.text: Open the budget to a closed session of parliament.
answers.sub: Deputies see the main figures in secret; businesses stay hidden.

reasons.mb: The people's deputies finally see where the money goes.
reasons.usa: Civilian oversight, the reform Washington quietly wants.
reasons.army: Civilian scrutiny of our budget is the red line.
reasons.salc: Nour shares a seat at the table.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh wants an army that answers to no Islamist.

answers.gripWhy: Elected deputies get a first look inside the army.

answers.text: Refuse: the army's budget is a national secret.
answers.sub: The army's economy stays one line, beyond parliament's reach.

reasons.army: Our budget and businesses stay ours.
reasons.moi: A Council that keeps its secrets keeps ours.
reasons.mb: Elected deputies shut out of a vast economy.
reasons.usa: Congress keeps paying for books it cannot see.
reasons.rev: The generals' empire stays above the people.

answers.gripWhy: The army's accounts sealed from the elected house.

situations.title: Morality Patrols
situations.question: Bearded men police the streets in God's name. Will you arrest them?
situations.body: From Suez, Alexandria and Cairo come reports of bearded men harassing couples, unveiled women and shops selling music. They call themselves a committee for the promotion of virtue and prevention of vice. The Nour Party denies any link. Salafist preachers defend the religious duty of commanding good.

answers.text: Arrest them; only the state keeps order.
answers.sub: Police round up the patrols and charge them under criminal law.

reasons.moi: Our streets, our authority; no bearded rivals.
reasons.fel: Order protects tourism and our shops.
reasons.salc: Preachers of good treated like criminals again.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh dislikes Egyptian police hunting pious men.
reasons.rev: Mubarak's police back in charge, on any excuse.

answers.gripWhy: Arrests and patrols restore police authority on the street.

answers.text: Let the sheikhs restrain their own young men.
answers.sub: No arrests; the Salafist Call promises to rein them in.

reasons.salc: Our sheikhs, not the police, guide our youth.
reasons.ksa: The pious are trusted to correct the pious.
reasons.moi: Tolerated vigilantes make the police a joke.
reasons.rev: Women harassed, and the state shrugs.
reasons.usa: Tourists and Copts at risk; Washington takes note.

answers.gripWhy: The state steps back and leaves preachers in charge.

answers.text: Try harassers in civil courts; protect personal freedom.
answers.sub: Public prosecutors, not mass arrests; women's and Copts' rights affirmed.

reasons.rev: Freedom in the street, defended by law.
reasons.usa: Rule of law for women and Copts.
reasons.salc: Secularists brand commanding good a crime.
reasons.moi: Civilian prosecutors instead of our methods.
reasons.mb: Freedom talk today means attacks on religion tomorrow.

situations.title: The Gas Contract
situations.question: The state gas company wants to cancel the Israel contract. Will you allow it?
situations.body: The Sinai pipeline has been bombed more than a dozen times since February 2011. Gas to Israel has stopped for months. EGAS, the state gas company, says the buyer owes money and moves to end the contract. Parliament cheers. Washington warns of damage to the peace. Old-regime contractors fear prosecution.

answers.text: Cancel the contract; Egyptian gas is not a gift.
answers.sub: Termination notice to the buyer; exports to Israel end.

reasons.rev: Mubarak's giveaway to Israel finally ends.
reasons.mb: Parliament's demand met, and our deputies get the credit.
reasons.usa: A blow to the 1979 peace Washington guarantees.
reasons.fel: Call the deal theft and our contractors face prosecution.
reasons.army: Strain on the treaty means strain on the aid.

answers.text: Call it a business dispute and renegotiate the price.
answers.sub: Arbitration and a higher price; the treaty kept out of it.

reasons.army: The treaty and the aid stay safe.
reasons.usa: Calm handling protects the peace Washington underwrites.
reasons.fel: No prosecutions if it stays commercial.
reasons.rev: The giveaway kept on Mubarak's terms.
reasons.mb: Parliament's will brushed aside by the generals.

situations.title: Siege at Abbasiya
situations.question: Your Defence Ministry is besieged. Will you send troops or let sheikhs mediate?
situations.body: Followers of the Salafist preacher Hazem Salah Abu Ismail have camped outside the Defence Ministry in Abbasiya since his candidacy was struck out. At dawn, armed men in plain clothes attacked the camp; at least 11 are dead. Revolutionaries and Brotherhood youth march in support. Armoured vehicles ring the gates.

answers.text: Impose a curfew; send the arrested to military prosecutors.
answers.sub: Troops clear Abbasiya; hundreds face military trials.

reasons.army: The ministry is defended and the army's dignity kept.
reasons.moi: Order restored, and our warnings proved right.
reasons.salc: Our brothers before military courts again.
reasons.rev: More civilians before military judges; the attackers untouched.
reasons.usa: Military trials Washington has condemned for a year.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh admires a Council that does not bend.

answers.gripWhy: Curfew and military trials for the arrested.

answers.text: Let Salafist sheikhs talk the camp into leaving peacefully.
answers.sub: Yasser Borhami's preachers talk the camp down; no military trials.

reasons.salc: We are the bridge between the state and its youth.
reasons.mb: No bloodbath the Islamist camp must answer for.
reasons.army: Generals bargaining with besiegers at their own gate.
reasons.moi: Sheikhs given a job meant for the police.
reasons.rev: No new prisoners for the military courts.

answers.gripWhy: No troops and no trials; sheikhs mediate instead.

situations.title: Qatar's Deposits
situations.question: Qatar offers $2 billion in deposits. Will you take Qatari money?
situations.body: Qatar offers $2 billion in Central Bank deposits, plus investment pledges for the Suez Canal zone. Its envoys speak openly of working with the next government, meaning the Brotherhood. Riyadh still owes much of its $4 billion pledge. It warns against letting Qatar gain a foothold.

answers.text: Accept Qatar's deposits and invite its investors.
answers.sub: Reserves eased; Qatar becomes the Brotherhood's banker in Cairo.

reasons.qat: Doha's money buys a seat at Cairo's table.
reasons.mb: Our ally steadies the economy we will inherit.
reasons.ksa: A Qatari foothold in Cairo is Riyadh's red line.
reasons.army: Qatari money buys the Brotherhood, not the state.
reasons.fel: Our Saudi partners pull away.

answers.text: Refuse Qatar; ask the Saudi-led Islamic Development Bank instead.
answers.sub: Smaller Islamic loans from Jeddah; Doha snubbed, Salafist friends pleased.

reasons.salc: The Call's Gulf friends keep their place.
reasons.ksa: Saudi-led money keeps Cairo in Riyadh's orbit.
reasons.qat: Doha's offer thrown back in its face.
reasons.mb: Our ally's money refused for Saudi strings.
reasons.rev: One Gulf master swapped for another.

answers.text: Take neither; the army's own funds defend the pound.
answers.sub: The army's businesses lend to the Central Bank; no Gulf strings.

reasons.army: The nation sees the army pay for its stability.
reasons.moi: Sovereign and strong, as the state should be.
reasons.qat: Doha's billions refused by the generals.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's leverage shrinks along with Doha's.
reasons.mb: A drained treasury left for us to inherit.

callbacks.title: Arbitration over the Gas
callbacks.question: Israel's buyers threaten to sue. Will you keep the gas shut off?
callbacks.body: You stopped gas exports to Israel after the pipeline bombing. East Mediterranean Gas, the export company, now threatens an international claim for billions. Washington's envoys mention the peace treaty. Delta factories short of fuel ask for the gas.

answers.text: Send the gas to Egyptian factories at state prices
answers.sub: Export gas goes to state factories and power plants.

reasons.rev: Egyptian gas fuels Egyptian workers, not Israeli plants.
reasons.army: Military factories get cheap gas too.
reasons.mb: Defying Israel's buyers plays well in every mosque.
reasons.usa: The treaty's economic pillar is abandoned.
reasons.fel: Contractors lose commissions and face the legal claim.

answers.text: Keep it shut; no fuel for Jerusalem's occupiers
answers.sub: Exports banned on religious grounds; the claim fought to the end.

reasons.salc: The preachers' ruling becomes state policy.
reasons.mb: The Brotherhood cannot look softer on Israel.
reasons.usa: A religious embargo on Israel enrages Congress.
reasons.army: Holy-war talk near Sinai is a soldier's nightmare.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh wants no wild adventures from Cairo.

callbacks.title: Principles or Rulings
callbacks.question: Will you keep 'principles of Sharia' in Article 2, or write 'rulings'?
callbacks.body: You made al-Azhar's Document the basis of the constitution. Now Salafist preachers want Article 2 to say 'the rulings of Sharia', the strict letter. They want al-Azhar's scholars to check every law. The Brotherhood wants 'principles' kept and parliament to decide. Coptic bishops warn of rule by clerics.

answers.text: Keep 'principles'; the elected parliament interprets them
answers.sub: The Document's wording holds; Islamist deputies will define Sharia.

reasons.mb: Elected deputies, mostly its own, will define Sharia.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies gain the power to interpret.
reasons.usa: The milder wording reassures Washington and the Copts.
reasons.salc: Vague principles leave Article 2 to politicians.
reasons.fel: An Islamist parliament defining Sharia threatens their business.

answers.text: Write 'rulings' and give al-Azhar's scholars a veto
answers.sub: Senior scholars check every law against Sharia.

reasons.salc: Sharia's rulings bind the state, as the ancestors taught.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh welcomes a stricter Sharia clause.
reasons.mb: Clerics, not its deputies, will judge the laws.
reasons.rev: A clerical veto buries the civil state.
reasons.usa: Washington hears rule by clerics in Egypt's constitution.

answers.gripWhy: Clerics' review narrows what any parliament may pass.

callbacks.title: Eid Meat from the Mosques
callbacks.question: Will you let Salafist mosques hand out the Eid meat and bread?
callbacks.body: In July you praised the Salafist Call's discipline in Tahrir. Now, before the Eid al-Adha feast, its preachers ask to hand out cheap state bread and Gulf-funded sacrifice meat through their mosques in Alexandria and the Delta. The state ration shops would stand aside.

answers.text: Let the mosques distribute; charity is a religious duty.
answers.sub: Gulf-funded Salafist committees hand out meat and ration bread.

reasons.salc: Every family our mosques feed remembers us at the polls.
reasons.ksa: Saudi charity reaches Egypt's poor through Riyadh's friends.
reasons.mb: The Salafists buy the poor vote the Brotherhood built.
reasons.rev: The state hands its bread to campaigning preachers.
reasons.fel: Our clans lose their hold on the poor to the sheikhs.

answers.text: Keep bread in the state ration shops, for all.
answers.sub: The supply ministry sells Eid meat at low prices nationwide.

reasons.army: The army's bakeries and the state keep feeding the people.
reasons.rev: Bread is a right, not a sheikh's favour.
reasons.mb: Better the state than the Salafists at the ration counter.
reasons.salc: The state shuts our charity to keep the poor dependent.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's charity refused at its friends' door.

callbacks.title: Bearded Guards at the Polls
callbacks.question: Will you keep the Salafist committees at the polling stations?
callbacks.body: In November you let Salafist neighbourhood committees guard the polls. Judges in Alexandria and Kafr el-Sheikh now report men in the queues telling voters which list God wants. The Brotherhood files complaints. Runoff votes open next week.

answers.text: Keep the committees; the pious keep better order.
answers.sub: Salafist volunteers stay at the stations through the runoffs.

reasons.salc: Our volunteers stand where the voters are.
reasons.ksa: Order kept by believers suits Riyadh.
reasons.mb: Salafist guards steer voters away from our lists.
reasons.moi: Bearded volunteers take over police authority.
reasons.usa: Observers report intimidation; the vote loses credibility.

answers.text: Send them home; let every party's agents watch.
answers.sub: Only judges and party agents supervise; Brotherhood agents everywhere.

reasons.mb: Our thousands of agents guard the ballot box properly.
reasons.usa: Party agents and judges look like a real election.
reasons.qat: A clean Islamist win, confirmed by the ballot.
reasons.salc: Our volunteers sent home so the Brotherhood watches alone.
reasons.moi: Party agents at every station undercut police supervision.

callbacks.title: The First Islamic Bond Sale
callbacks.question: Gulf banks want Suez Canal income as security. Will you allow it?
callbacks.body: You backed the Nour Party's sukuk bill. Sukuk are Islamic bonds. The first sale is ready. Saudi and Qatari banks want Suez Canal income and state land as security. Nasserist deputies recall the khedive's debts of 1875. The Brotherhood's party wants to name the Sharia board that approves the bonds.

answers.text: Back the bonds with taxes, never the canal
answers.sub: Smaller sale; no foreign claim on Suez or public land.

reasons.rev: The canal stays the people's, as in 1956.
reasons.army: No foreign claim on our country's own ground.
reasons.salc: Weak bonds that the Gulf buyers will refuse.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's banks refuse such a weak guarantee.
reasons.qat: Doha's banks see poor returns.

answers.text: Pledge canal income; let the Sharia board approve
answers.sub: Gulf banks buy it all; Salafist scholars sit on the board.

reasons.salc: Our scholars now guard the state's money.
reasons.ksa: Saudi banks gain a claim on the canal.
reasons.army: A foreign claim on the canal touches our sovereignty.
reasons.rev: The khedive's debt trap again, in Islamic dress.
reasons.mb: Nour's scholars sit on the board, not ours.

answers.text: Let Freedom and Justice name the Sharia board
answers.sub: A Brotherhood committee runs the sales; Qatari banks buy first.

reasons.mb: Islamic finance under the majority party's control.
reasons.qat: Doha's banks lead the first sale.
reasons.salc: The Brotherhood steals the bill we wrote.
reasons.ksa: Doha's banks push Riyadh's aside.
reasons.fel: Party committees running state debt scare the bankers.

callbacks.title: Patrols in Suez
callbacks.question: The patrols are spreading. Will you back neighbourhood guards or the sheikhs?
callbacks.body: You left the self-appointed virtue patrols to the sheikhs. Now they stop buses and close cafés in Suez and Ismailiya. A music shop has been burned. Neighbourhood committees from the January uprising offer to guard the streets. The Salafist Call says its own stewards will do it.

answers.text: Revive the neighbourhood committees under local councils
answers.sub: Workers and local men patrol with council badges, not police.

reasons.rev: The street belongs to its people again.
reasons.moi: Civilian patrols take the police's job.
reasons.salc: Leftist gangs set against the pious.
reasons.army: Organised civilians are a danger to order.
reasons.fel: Workers' committees scare business.

answers.gripWhy: Neighbourhoods police themselves without the security state.

answers.text: Let Salafist stewards patrol beside the police
answers.sub: Salafist Call stewards patrol with police, on the sheikhs' word.

reasons.salc: The Call is recognised as guardian of the streets.
reasons.ksa: Pious order in Egypt's towns pleases Riyadh.
reasons.moi: Bearded volunteers placed over our officers' heads.
reasons.rev: Morality militias, now with official blessing.
reasons.usa: Badged vigilantes alarm Washington and the Copts.
reasons.mb: Nour wins the streets the Brotherhood wanted.

pending.line: Omar Suleiman has been without office since Mubarak's fall, yet the General Intelligence directorate he ran still holds the regime's files. Sami Anan urges the Field Marshal to sideline him and take the service under the Council. Riyadh and Washington prize him as their trusted channel to Cairo.

Central Bank Governor Farouk el-Okdah reports that Mubarak-era tycoons and foreign portfolio funds are draining dollars while the stock exchange stays shut. The Council must choose between capital controls with travel bans on businessmen, and open markets to reassure investors and the Gulf.

Mohamed Badie asks for a Brotherhood jurist on the committee drafting the constitutional amendments, which would amount to public recognition of the movement. The youth coalition and the liberal parties object to one movement holding a seat. The Salafist Call watches for any word on Article 2.

Crowds have broken into State Security Investigations headquarters at Nasr City and found files shredded and burnt. The new Interior Minister Mansour el-Essawy asks the Council to choose: dissolve the service and hand the surviving files to prosecutors, or rename it and keep its officers.

The revolutionaries, the Brotherhood and Washington demand a firm date for lifting the Emergency Law of the Mubarak years. The Interior Ministry insists it needs emergency powers while its police are still off the streets.

A mob has burnt the church at Sol in Atfih, and Copts are camped outside the Maspero building. Salafist sheikhs offer a customary reconciliation session. Pope Shenouda III's bishops and the revolutionaries demand prosecutions and a church rebuilt by the army.

Khairat al-Shater and other Brotherhood leaders are serving military-court sentences from the Mubarak years. Mohamed Badie asks for their release. The Interior Ministry warns of an emboldened Brotherhood, and Riyadh is alarmed.
The revolutionaries demand that leaders of the National Democratic Party be barred from the coming elections. Ahmed Shafik's allies and the provincial clans propose rebranding the party instead.

In Qena, Salafist preachers lead crowds blocking the railway against the new governor, a Copt and former police general. Essam Sharaf's cabinet asks the Council to stand by the appointment, freeze it, or send troops to reopen the line.

With its Freedom and Justice Party now founded, the Brotherhood asks for legal registration of the Society itself and its Muqattam headquarters. The Interior Ministry still keeps its old files on every member.

The Foreign Ministry floats restoring relations with Iran, and Egyptian intelligence prepares to host a Fatah-Hamas reconciliation. Riyadh and Washington frown. Nasserists, the Brotherhood and Doha cheer a foreign policy freed from Mubarak's alignments.

Military censors tell editors to clear every article about the armed forces in advance, and a blogger and a television host are summoned for insulting the army. The independent dailies, Al Jazeera and the US State Department protest.

Salafist crowds besieged churches in Imbaba over rumours of a convert held inside, and the night ended in deaths and a burnt church. Copts now demand the long-promised unified law on places of worship, and the Salafist Call rejects it. The Interior Ministry wants special powers in Giza.
Hamas and the Brotherhood press for the Rafah crossing into Gaza to open permanently. Washington and Israel warn against it, and the army fears for Sinai. Doha offers to fund the traffic.

Riyadh's $4 billion pledge must now take shape. Farouk el-Okdah wants Central Bank deposits to defend the pound, Riyadh prefers project grants released tranche by tranche at its discretion, and the generals want military-economy projects included.

Emad Abdel Ghafour's Nour Party applies for a licence, but the parties law bans parties founded on religion. The Brotherhood would rather not share the Islamist vote. Gulf-trained preachers promise a mass following.

Families of the martyrs camp in Tahrir. Mansour el-Essawy now proposes retiring hundreds of police generals and suspending officers charged with killing protesters. The ranks threaten to stay home and ask the Field Marshal to block the purge.

Essam Sharaf's cabinet drafts the first budget since the revolution. The unions demand a national minimum wage and permanent contracts for temporary workers. The business elite and Washington's economists warn of the deficit and falling reserves.

Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's Military Intelligence brings a dossier on foreign funding of April 6 and the rights groups, from American democracy institutes to Gulf donors. Publishing it and opening a judicial inquiry would brand the youth as agents and anger Washington.

Deputy Prime Minister Ali al-Selmi drafts supra-constitutional principles to bind the future constituent assembly. Sami Anan wants clauses keeping the military budget beyond parliament. The Brotherhood and the Salafists warn of the street.

Administrative courts annul Mubarak-era sales of public companies and state land. Workers demand renationalisation, while the tycoons and Gulf investors who bought the assets demand that the state appeal.

After crowds stormed the Israeli embassy, the Interior Ministry asks the Council to reactivate and widen the Emergency Law to cover strikes, road blocking and 'spreading rumours'. Revolutionaries and Washington see the promised lifting buried.

With the vote weeks away, revolutionaries and the Brotherhood demand the revived Treachery Law to bar former ruling-party officials. Old-party families in Upper Egypt threaten to block roads and railways if it is applied.

Twenty-eight Copts died at Maspero under army vehicles while state television urged citizens to defend the army, and the military prosecution has claimed the inquiry. Copts, revolutionaries and Washington demand a civilian investigation and accountability for the broadcast.

Riyadh slows its tranches while Gulf charities and preachers pour money into the Salafist Call's campaign. Restricting private Gulf funding of parties risks the Saudi deposits; tolerating it hands the Salafists an army of volunteers.

The al-Selmi document is now public. The Salafist Call and the Brotherhood call a mass Friday against it and demand the withdrawal of the clauses on military autonomy and on the constituent assembly. Sami Anan wants them kept, and the youth join the march.

As the Nour Party surges in the polls, its leaders call for segregated beaches and limits on alcohol for tourists. Hotel and tourism tycoons demand public reassurance from the Council. Salafist preachers warn the state not to defy the people's choice.

Security forces raided 17 democracy and rights groups, American institutes among them, and prosecutors now move to charge their staff. Washington demands the property back and hints at the aid. The Interior Ministry and Military Intelligence call it sovereignty.

For the uprising's first anniversary, the Field Marshal can lift the Emergency Law entirely, lift it except for 'thuggery', or keep it. Interior Minister Mohamed Ibrahim Youssef wants the exception kept; revolutionaries call it a loophole for everything.

The People's Assembly convenes under Speaker Saad al-Katatni with an Islamist majority. The Brotherhood demands the right to dismiss Kamal Ganzouri and form a government, and the Nour Party wants ministries too. The Council's declaration gives parliament no such power.

After 74 died at Port Said while police stood by, Ultras besiege the Interior Ministry. The People's Assembly demands Mohamed Ibrahim Youssef's dismissal and a full restructuring of the police. The ranks warn of a strike if officers are prosecuted.

Sixteen Americans are under a travel ban and US senators threaten the $1.3 billion in aid. Washington proposes bail and quiet departure. Nationalist papers and Brotherhood deputies demand the trial proceed, and the generals weigh the aid against their pride.

Generals and old-party men urge Omar Suleiman to stand for president as the state's candidate, though Sami Anan nurses ambitions of his own. Riyadh likes the former intelligence chief. Washington and the Brotherhood would see a restoration.

Deputies reject Kamal Ganzouri's programme, and the Brotherhood threatens to run its own presidential candidate unless it may form a government. The Council can keep Ganzouri, reshuffle with Brotherhood ministers, or call the bluff.

The Islamist majority fills the 100-member constituent assembly largely with its own. Liberals, al-Azhar and the Coptic Church walk out, and lawyers petition the courts. The Council can intervene, wait on the judges, or bless the assembly.

The Brotherhood nominates Khairat al-Shater for president, but his Mubarak-era military-court conviction may bar him unless the Field Marshal grants full rehabilitation. Doha favours him and Riyadh dreads him.

Parliament has passed a political isolation law aimed at Omar Suleiman and Ahmed Shafik. The Field Marshal must ratify it, refer it to the Supreme Constitutional Court, or sit on it as the candidate list closes.

Farouk Sultan's commission has disqualified ten candidates, among them Hazem Salah Abu Ismail, Khairat al-Shater and Omar Suleiman. Abu Ismail's followers besiege the commission. The Council must back its ruling or reopen appeals.

Protesters besiege the Saudi embassy over an Egyptian lawyer detained in the kingdom, and Riyadh recalls its ambassador with much of the pledge still undelivered. The Salafist Call and the business elite urge an apology; the revolutionaries demand the lawyer's release.

Ahmed Shafik and Mohamed Morsi head to the runoff. Old-party networks, police and state television line up behind Shafik, and the Brotherhood warns of fraud. The Field Marshal decides how neutral the state will appear.
Hamdeen Sabahi, third in the first round, demands a recount and the suspension of the runoff, and his Nasserist and youth supporters fill Tahrir. Both runoff camps court his voters.

Mamdouh Shahin drafts a supplementary constitutional declaration reserving military affairs to the Council, and legislative power too should parliament fall, after the handover. The Brotherhood and Washington would call it a soft coup.

Farouk Sultan's Supreme Constitutional Court hears the challenge to the election law, and Islamist deputies move a bill curbing the court. The Council must decide whether to defend the judges or bargain with a parliament it may soon lose.
